text: When you document something you just built, it's tempting to write the version that makes sense to you, right now, with every decision still fresh in your head. That version is fast to write and feels complete, but it's only complete for a reader who already has your context -- and the whole point of documentation is to reach a reader who doesn't, whether that's you in six months or a new hire today.

The gap between adequate documentation and genuinely useful documentation almost always comes down to one missing ingredient: the reasoning behind a decision, not just the decision itself. Writing 'Subnet: 10.0.1.0/24' tells a reader what exists. Adding that a /24 was chosen over a smaller /28 specifically to leave room for roughly 3x growth within a year tells them why -- and that's the version that lets a future engineer reason about the subnet later instead of just staring at a number.

A practical way to check your own documentation before calling it finished: imagine a new hire, with no access to you, reading only what you wrote. Could they understand the decision and operate around it without sending you a message? If you can picture the exact question they'd have to ask -- why is this a /24 and not something smaller -- that question is the sentence missing from your notes, and it belongs in the document, not in a Slack thread six months from now.

The same test applies well beyond subnet sizing. A VM size documented with the baseline load it covers and the batch-job spike that justified sizing up a tier gives a future engineer something to reason from. A backup retention window documented with the compliance minimum and the buffer added on top does the same. In every case, the why turns a plain fact into something the next engineer can actually use.

Write for the person who isn't you yet, and most of this course's remaining documentation work gets easier. Next, closing this chapter with a concrete handoff checklist that pulls everything from diagrams to the new-hire test into one practical list.
